commercially in the UK, and the regulatory pathway for routine beyond visual line of sight (BVLOS) flight is opening. National law gives local authorities no general power to set flight routes, restrict airspace or license commercial use of the airspace above their areas. The Civil Aviation Act 1982, the Air Navigation Order 2016 and the Air Traffic Management and Unmanned Aircraft Act 2021 place those functions with the Secretary of State and the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA). Councils do, however, control the ground: launch sites, hubs and vertiports need planning permission. Recent decisions in Darlington and, in the Republic of Ireland, in Fingal, County Dublin, show that planning control is already being used as a proxy for airspace governance, with consequences ranging from capped flight rates to an operator ceasing service altogether. This article makes three arguments. First, the gap between local land-use control and national airspace control leaves residents without a proportionate local route to influence where and how often drones fly over them, and private-law remedies are largely closed off by statute. Second, planning control is too blunt to fill that gap: it can refuse or condition a site, but it cannot address routes, overflown neighbourhoods or the cumulative effect of several operators. Third, comparisons with airport noise, battery energy storage systems (BESS) and telecommunications masts suggest that unresolved conflicts of this kind harden over time. The article argues for digital tools that let councils translate planning policy into machine-readable airspace constraints within the existing national framework, and for legislative reform to give local authorities a defined statutory In Canada, such operations are governed by Standard 922, which states safety targets and identifies ARP4761 as an acceptable means of compliance. However, existing safety practice is insufficient, as it was developed for crewed aircraft and rests on assumptions that are no longer valid for RPAS. Existing practice also fixes the evidence at the point of declaration, while the aircraft and its components continue to age. This research develops a system safety assessment framework for RPAS with vertical take-off and landing (VTOL) and cruise capability that assigns criticality from the terminal outcome of a failure rather than from functional loss. The proposed framework is structured as an iterative five-phase process, adapted from ARP4761, and introduces an intermediate layer of critical events that separates architecture-dependent from consequence-dependent analysis. The resulting fault tree is then extended into a health-informed, time-varying assessment in which each basic event is evaluated at the current age or observed condition of the component and tested against a dispatch threshold derived from the certification target, which has practical applications for operators assessing the fitness of an individual aircraft in service. A case study was conducted on a representative hybrid VTOL-cruise platform to demonstrate and evaluate the framework's perpetual, non-exclusive license"}],"descriptions":[{"descriptionType":"Abstract","description":"Beyond Visual Line of Sight (BVLOS) unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) operations increasingly use 5G standalone (SA) networks for command and control (C2) between the UAV and the ground control station (GCS). The 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) has specified mechanisms for authentication and authorization of unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) in this architectural setting. As a result, operators may treat registration state, Protocol Data Unit (PDU) session status, and IP reachability as evidence that the C2 path is available. In practice, however, these connectivity indicators alone do not guarantee that closed-loop control remains operationally safe. Attacks can degrade UAS C2 when timeliness degrades under shared User Plane contention, mobility continuity fails during Control Plane instability, or command integrity is violated at a trusted next-generation Node B (gNodeB). Such failures undermine connectivity as the central security indicator for UAV operations. In this paper, we demonstrate these issues using three distinct threat models on a reproducible Open5GS and UERANSIM testbed that carries Micro Air Vehicle Link (MAVLink) over the 5G User Plane, and we use a commercial Nokia core to ground deployment assumptions. We address timeliness, availability, and integrity through experiments in which attack success is defined as forcing an unsafe closed-loop state without a clean disconnect. We observe stale telemetry and heavy-tailed delay under co-tenant User Plane contention, failsafe after handover under Control Plane instability, and navigation hijacking after command rewriting at a compromised gNodeB. We further discuss why each threat model arises and evaluate mitigations for these cross-layer failures. Across the study, we disclosed five robustness issues, all with assigned CVEs."}],"geoLocations":[],"fundingReferences":[],"url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.04662","contentUrl":null,"metadataVersion":4,"schemaVersion":"http://datacite.org/schema/kernel-4","source":"mds","isActive":true,"state":"findable","reason":null,"viewCount":0,"downloadCount":0,"referenceCount":0,"citationCount":0,"partCount":0,"partOfCount":0,"versionCount":0,"versionOfCount":0,"created":"2026-03-06T02:58:04Z","registered":"2026-03-06T02:58:05Z","published":null,"updated":"2026-11-13T09:09:23Z"},"relationships":{"client":{"data":{"id":"arxiv.content","type":"clients"}}}}],"meta":{"total":304,"totalPages":51,"page":1},"links":{"self":"https://api.datacite.org/dois?query=%28%22%D1%82%D1%80%D0%BE%D0%BF%D0%BE%D1%81%D1%84%D0%B5%D1%80%D0%BD%D0%B0%D1%8F%20%D1%81%D0%B2%D1%8F%D0%B7%D1%8C%22%20OR%20%22%D1%82%D1%80%D0%BE%D0%BF%D0%BE%D1%81%D1%84%D0%B5%D1%80%D0%BD%D0%BE%D0%B5%20%D1%80%D0%B0%D1%81%D1%81%D0%B5%D1%8F%D0%BD%D0%B8%D0%B5%22%20OR%20%22%D1%82%D1%80%D0%BE%D0%BF%D0%BE%D1%81%D1%84%D0%B5%D1%80%D0%BD%D0%B0%D1%8F%20%D1%80%D0%B0%D0%B4%D0%B8%D0%BE%D1%81%D0%B2%D1%8F%D0%B7%D1%8C%22%20OR%20%22%D0%B7%D0%B0%D0%B3%D0%BE%D1%80%D0%B8%D0%B7%D0%BE%D0%BD%D1%82%D0%BD%D0%B0%D1%8F%20%D1%81%D0%B2%D1%8F%D0%B7%D1%8C%22%29%20OR%20%28%22tropospheric%20scatter%22%20OR%20troposcatter%20OR%20%22tropospheric%20radio%20propagation%22%20OR%20%22beyond%20line%20of%20sight%22%29\u0026page%5Bsize%5D=6","next":"https://api.datacite.org/dois?page%5Bnumber%5D=2\u0026page%5Bsize%5D=6\u0026query=%28%22%D1%82%D1%80%D0%BE%D0%BF%D0%BE%D1%81%D1%84%D0%B5%D1%80%D0%BD%D0%B0%D1%8F+%D1%81%D0%B2%D1%8F%D0%B7%D1%8C%22+OR+%22%D1%82%D1%80%D0%BE%D0%BF%D0%BE%D1%81%D1%84%D0%B5%D1%80%D0%BD%D0%BE%D0%B5+%D1%80%D0%B0%D1%81%D1%81%D0%B5%D1%8F%D0%BD%D0%B8%D0%B5%22+OR+%22%D1%82%D1%80%D0%BE%D0%BF%D0%BE%D1%81%D1%84%D0%B5%D1%80%D0%BD%D0%B0%D1%8F+%D1%80%D0%B0%D0%B4%D0%B8%D0%BE%D1%81%D0%B2%D1%8F%D0%B7%D1%8C%22+OR+%22%D0%B7%D0%B0%D0%B3%D0%BE%D1%80%D0%B8%D0%B7%D0%BE%D0%BD%D1%82%D0%BD%D0%B0%D1%8F+%D1%81%D0%B2%D1%8F%D0%B7%D1%8C%22%29+OR+%28%2
